title: Euronaval 2026: France Orders 32-Cell Aster Missile Upgrade for FDI Frigates
summary: France has placed an official order for a 32-cell Vertical Launch System (VLS) upgrade for its FDI frigates. This enhancement, announced at Euronaval 2026, will double the frigates' air defense capacity by allowing them to carry more Aster missiles.
detail:
France has ordered a significant upgrade for its new Frégate de Défense et d'Intervention (FDI) frigates, doubling their Vertical Launch System (VLS) capacity from 16 to 32 cells for Aster surface-to-air missiles. This announcement, made at Euronaval 2026, means the frigates will carry twice as many interceptors.

This enhancement is crucial for several reasons. Doubling the VLS cells dramatically increases the frigates' air defense capabilities, allowing them to counter more numerous or complex aerial threats, such as advanced anti-ship missiles, aircraft, or drone swarms, over a sustained period. The Aster 30 missile, which these frigates will primarily use, provides area air defense, meaning the ships can protect not only themselves but also other valuable assets within a naval task group. This upgrade signals France's recognition of an evolving and more challenging threat landscape in modern naval warfare, requiring more robust and resilient defensive systems for its frontline warships.

The FDI frigates are a new class of multi-role vessels intended to be the backbone of the French Navy's surface fleet, replacing older ships. Their original design already incorporated advanced stealth features and combat systems. The decision to enhance their missile capacity before full deployment underscores a strategic imperative to future-proof these critical assets against increasingly sophisticated adversaries and ensure their effectiveness in high-intensity conflicts. This move aligns with a broader trend among global navies to bolster air and missile defense capabilities.

title: Operational F-15EXs Have Started Flying With Conformal Fuel Tanks
summary: Operational F-15EX fighter jets have begun flying with Conformal Fuel Tanks (CFTs). While the U.S. Air Force initially did not plan for the air-to-air focused F-15EX to use CFTs, evolving mission requirements have led to their integration.
detail:
Operational F-15EX Eagle II fighter jets have begun flying with Conformal Fuel Tanks (CFTs), a significant development given the U.S. Air Force's initial plans for the aircraft. The F-15EX was primarily conceived as an air-to-air combat platform, leveraging its speed and payload capacity to complement stealth fighters. The adoption of CFTs indicates an evolution in its mission demands.

Conformal Fuel Tanks are semi-permanently attached fuel tanks that conform to the aircraft's fuselage, offering a substantial increase in fuel capacity without occupying weapon pylons. This is crucial because it allows the F-15EX to maintain its full weapon carriage capability while significantly extending its operational range and endurance. This extended reach is vital for potential operations across vast distances, particularly in the Indo-Pacific theater, where aerial refueling assets might be contested or scarce. Longer endurance also means the aircraft can loiter over targets or patrol areas for extended periods.

While CFTs add some weight and drag, potentially impacting extreme performance metrics, the trade-off is deemed acceptable for missions prioritizing range, payload, and sustained presence. This move enhances the F-15EX's versatility, transforming it into an even more adaptable multi-role platform capable of undertaking a wider array of missions, including long-range strike or reconnaissance, in addition to its primary air superiority role. It underscores the Air Force's strategic shift towards greater operational flexibility and reach in a complex global security environment.

title: Treasury Cuts Crypto Exchange MEXC Off From US Financial System
summary: The U.S. Treasury's FinCEN has issued an order, as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' to bar U.S. financial institutions from processing transfers to or from MEXC. The Treasury alleges that MEXC facilitated $16 billion in illicit finance linked to entities in Iran, North Korea, and Russia. This action effectively severs MEXC from the U.S. financial system.
